subject: ACC
label: Grade 11 Commerce
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 11 Commerce Accountancy, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 6 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.
standard: Each unit: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown. Course pass: no unit at 'Not yet' after one retry, and a pass in SA1 and SA2.

modules.title: Accounting concepts and the accounting equation
modules.outcome: apply accounting principles and the accounting equation
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Accounting concepts and the accounting equation', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: apply accounting principles and the accounting equation. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Read the idea in 'Accounting concepts and the accounting equation' and tie it to a small real business, such as a school shop or a family stall.
Write the rule or format in your own words and keep one clean example.
Use it: apply accounting principles and the accounting equation. Work from source papers or a short story of transactions.
Check it: totals agree, each entry has a reason, and every figure can be traced.
modules.example: Solved: Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Cash 5,000 + Stock 3,000 = Loan 2,000 + Capital 6,000. If the owner pays 1,000 of the loan in cash: Assets 7,000 = Liabilities 1,000 + Capital 6,000. Method: Model run for 'Accounting concepts and the accounting equation'. Story: a small shop starts the month with cash and stock and has a short list of transactions. Step 1, list each transaction and what it changes. Step 2, record it in the format of the unit. Step 3, total and check that both sides agree. Step 4, write one sentence about what the figures tell the owner. What a good answer looks like: every transaction is recorded in the right place, totals agree, and the sentence states a useful message. Use local money units and local rules.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Apply accounting principles and the accounting equation: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.

modules.title: Depreciation, provisions and reserves
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Depreciation, provisions and reserves', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: calculate depreciation and record provisions. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Read the idea in 'Depreciation, provisions and reserves' and tie it to a small real business, such as a school shop or a family stall.
Write the rule or format in your own words and keep one clean example.
Use it: calculate depreciation and record provisions. Work from source papers or a short story of transactions.
Check it: totals agree, each entry has a reason, and every figure can be traced.
modules.example: Solved: Machine cost 50,000, scrap value 5,000, life 5 years. Straight line: (50,000 - 5,000) / 5 = 9,000 per year. Method: Model run for 'Depreciation, provisions and reserves'. Story: a small shop starts the month with cash and stock and has a short list of transactions. Step 1, list each transaction and what it changes. Step 2, record it in the format of the unit. Step 3, total and check that both sides agree. Step 4, write one sentence about what the figures tell the owner. What a good answer looks like: every transaction is recorded in the right place, totals agree, and the sentence states a useful message. Use local money units and local rules.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Calculate depreciation and record provisions: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Straight-line depreciation: A machine costs 120,000, has an estimated scrap value of 20,000 and a life of 5 years. Annual depreciation is (120,000 minus 20,000) divided by 5, which is 20,000 each year, so the machine falls to 100,000 after year one.

Step 2, Journal entry: Depreciation A/c Dr 20,000, To Machinery A/c 20,000, being depreciation charged for the year. At year end Depreciation A/c Dr is closed by transfer: Profit and Loss A/c Dr 20,000, To Depreciation A/c 20,000.

Step 3, Reducing balance at 20 percent: Year 1 charge is 20 percent of 120,000, which is 24,000, leaving 96,000. Year 2 is 20 percent of 96,000, which is 19,200, leaving 76,800. Year 3 is 20 percent of 76,800, which is 15,360.

Step 4, Bad debts and provision: Debtors are 50,000. Bad debts of 2,000 are written off: Bad Debts A/c Dr 2,000, To Debtors A/c 2,000. Debtors become 48,000. A 5 percent provision is 48,000 times 5 percent, which is 2,400.

Step 5, Record the provision: Profit and Loss A/c Dr 2,400, To Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c 2,400. Balance sheet shows debtors 48,000 less provision 2,400, net 45,600. Next year, with debtors 60,000 and bad debts 1,000, the provision is 5 percent of 59,000, which is 2,950, so the extra charge is 550.

Step 6, Reserve: From a profit of 40,000, the owner sets aside 10,000. Entry: Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c Dr 10,000, To General Reserve A/c 10,000. This keeps 10,000 in the business without changing cash. The remaining 30,000 stays available.

Your turn: Equipment 80,000, scrap 8,000, life 6 years; debtors 40,000 with 1,000 bad debts and a 5 percent provision. Model answer: depreciation (80,000 minus 8,000) divided by 6 is 12,000; provision is 5 percent of 39,000, which is 1,950; Bad Debts Dr 1,000 To Debtors 1,000.

modules.title: Accounting with computers and spreadsheets
modules.outcome: record and report using accounting software
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Accounting with computers and spreadsheets', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: record and report using accounting software. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Read the idea in 'Accounting with computers and spreadsheets' and tie it to a small real business, such as a school shop or a family stall.
Write the rule or format in your own words and keep one clean example.
Use it: record and report using accounting software. Work from source papers or a short story of transactions.
Check it: totals agree, each entry has a reason, and every figure can be traced.
modules.example: Solved: Enter debits in column B and credits in column C. =SUM(B2:B10) and =SUM(C2:C10); the trial balance agrees if both totals match. Method: Model run for 'Accounting with computers and spreadsheets'. Story: a small shop starts the month with cash and stock and has a short list of transactions. Step 1, list each transaction and what it changes. Step 2, record it in the format of the unit. Step 3, total and check that both sides agree. Step 4, write one sentence about what the figures tell the owner. What a good answer looks like: every transaction is recorded in the right place, totals agree, and the sentence states a useful message. Use local money units and local rules.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Record and report using accounting software: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Set up accounts: In a spreadsheet Hana creates a sheet called Ledger with columns Account, Debit, Credit. She enters Cash 15,000 Dr, Debtors 8,000 Dr, Purchases 8,000 Dr, Rent 3,000 Dr, Capital 10,000 Cr, Sales 20,000 Cr, Creditors 4,000 Cr.

Step 2, Total with formulas: In B9 she types =SUM(B2:B5), which adds Cash, Debtors, Purchases and Rent to 34,000. In C9 she types =SUM(C6:C8) for Capital, Sales and Creditors, giving 34,000. The two totals agree, so the trial balance balances.

Step 3, Record a new transaction: A journal-style row records rent: Rent Dr 3,000, Cash Cr 3,000. In accounting software the click path is Transactions, New journal, choose date, select accounts, enter 3,000 on each side and Post. Rent rises, Cash falls.

Step 4, Check the effect: After posting rent, debits and credits still match because every journal has equal debit and credit lines. If she typed 3,000 against Rent but 300 against Cash, the software would refuse to post or show a difference of 2,700.

Step 5, Profit report: In a Profit and Loss sheet she types =C7-B4-B5 using Sales, Purchases and Rent cells, which is 20,000 minus 8,000 minus 3,000 and equals 9,000. The software report Reports, Profit and Loss would show the same 9,000.

Step 6, Protect and back up: She locks the formula cells, saves a copy named ledger-term1, and keeps an audit note of who entered what. Computers speed up arithmetic, but checking the trial balance remains the accountant's job.

Your turn: Cash 6,000 Dr, Sales 9,000 Cr, Capital 5,000 Cr, Purchases 4,000 Dr, Rent 2,000 Dr, Debtors 2,000 Dr. Does it balance? Model answer: Dr is 6,000 plus 4,000 plus 2,000 plus 2,000, which is 14,000; Cr is 9,000 plus 5,000, which is 14,000; yes, and profit is 9,000 minus 4,000 minus 2,000, or 3,000.

Which action verb starts the outcome of Unit 1 (Accounting concepts and the accounting equation), and at which Bloom level is it?
'apply', at the Apply level.
When do the formative checks FA1 to FA4 and the summative checks SA1 and SA2 happen?
FA1 to FA4 around weeks 6, 12, 24 and 30; SA1 in week 18; SA2 in week 36.

What evidence do you keep for each unit, and why?
A timed paper and an error log. It shows what you can really do and lets a teacher check it against the standard.
